state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Actually, in this case, alternate angles are not always equal. Alternate angles are formed when a transversal intersects two lines, and they are equal only when the lines are parallel. Since we don't know if the lines are parallel in this scenario, we cannot assume that angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. It's important to remember the specific conditions under which alternate angles are equal.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I see! So alternate angles are only equal if the lines are parallel. But how can I tell if the lines are parallel just by looking at a diagram? Do I need to look for something specific?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: To determine if the lines are parallel in a diagram, you can look for corresponding angles or alternate angles that are equal. If you find a pair of alternate angles that are equal, then you can conclude that the lines are parallel. Remember, parallel lines have special angle relationships that can help you identify them in a diagram.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, that makes sense! So if I see that some alternate angles are equal, then I can say the lines are parallel. But what if I don’t see any equal angles? How can I tell for sure if the lines are parallel or not?
